# Factorize

A development environment for your agent: use an authorized API, give a VM scoped access, or react to an Event.

Application: https://app.factorize.sh
MCP (Streamable HTTP + OAuth): https://app.factorize.sh/mcp

Factorize publishes Event occurrences; subscribers decide what to do with them.

Generated from maintained guides in navigation order. Do not edit this file directly.

## Factorize
Source: https://docs.factorize.sh/

Factorize is a development environment for your agent. Connect the services it
needs, approve just the access it should have, and see and revoke that access
in [Factorize](https://app.factorize.sh).

- **Use an API.** Your agent calls the APIs of connected services through MCP.
  Factorize uses the credentials you connected without handing them to the agent.
- **Give a VM access.** Give a supported workload its own scoped Factorize
  access, separate from the agent connection.
- **React to an event.** Use webhook or schedule Triggers, optionally combining
  inputs and authorized lookups before publishing an Event occurrence.
  Factorize publishes; the subscriber decides what to do with the occurrence.

[Try one of the three pathways](https://docs.factorize.sh/quickstart) or [look up MCP and REST](https://docs.factorize.sh/mcp/tools).

## Your first steps
Source: https://docs.factorize.sh/quickstart

In [Factorize](https://app.factorize.sh), select the team you want to use. In
your agent's MCP client, add the remote endpoint
`https://app.factorize.sh/mcp` and follow the sign-in prompt.

Factorize shows a consent page with the permissions you can approve. Select
only what the task needs and leave the rest unchecked. The browser's
**Clients** shows the connection afterward. If the task needs more
access later, review the new permissions in the browser; start Reconnect in the client,
then choose the same connection in Factorize to get a fresh credential. [Connection help](https://docs.factorize.sh/mcp/overview)

Pick one path. You do not need to complete all three.

## Use an API

If you have no connected service, open **Integrations** in Factorize and
connect one you own using a sandbox or test project. Approve a read-only
permission where the provider offers it, and approve access to that integration
for your agent. Do not paste credentials into the chat.

> Find an API I have connected in Factorize. Tell me which one you found, then
> make one read-only request against my test project. Show me the status and a
> short summary. Do not change anything or show credentials.

Success is a status and a result you recognize from the test project, not just
a list of tools. No provider record needs deleting. To remove temporary access,
update the client's permissions or delete the test integration from Factorize if nothing
else needs it. [Agent recipe](https://docs.factorize.sh/work/use-an-api)

## Give a VM access

Use a disposable Fly.io Machine on a Factorize deployment with [VM enrollment](https://docs.factorize.sh/work/vm-access) enabled.
Connect Fly.io in **Integrations** first. Review the client's VM
permissions on Factorize's consent page and approve only the grant described
below. Do not use a shared or production VM for the example.

> Ask me which test VM to use. Give just that VM permission to read Factorize
> Events. From inside the VM, list the team's Events to verify it works. Do not
> grant any other permissions or create or delete a VM.

An empty Event list from inside the VM counts as success. In Factorize, review
the active grant, then ask the agent to revoke that exact grant and confirm it
is gone. Revoking Factorize access does not stop the VM. [Agent recipe](https://docs.factorize.sh/work/vm-access)

## React to an event

Approve permission to read and write test Events and Triggers. Start with a
manual Trigger so you do not need a webhook provider or a scheduled job.

> Create a test Event named hello.factorize with a manual Trigger. If this
> client can subscribe to it, subscribe before firing. Fire it once with
> message "hello" and show me the saved occurrence. Do not send a notification
> or run another job.

Success is a saved occurrence you can also find in **Events**. A client that
cannot subscribe can still read the saved occurrence. When done, unsubscribe
if applicable, then have the agent delete only the test Event. Deleting an Event
also deletes its attached Triggers and stored occurrences. [Agent recipe](https://docs.factorize.sh/work/triggers)

## Connect your agent
Source: https://docs.factorize.sh/mcp/overview

Use Factorize's remote Streamable HTTP endpoint in your MCP client:

```text
https://app.factorize.sh/mcp
```

Factorize uses OAuth. Sign in, review the scopes shown, and approve only the
permissions needed for the task. A team can mark permissions as defaults for
new consent. Defaults are suggestions, not changes to existing grants; explicit
a new connection stays within an explicit client scope request. To replace an
existing credential, start Reconnect in your client and select that same
connection in the Factorize consent page. You can approve its available saved
permissions even when the client requests fewer at sign-in. The response lists
the actual scopes issued. A client that separately narrows the token request
or rejects the returned scopes may still need changes. Existing tokens never
gain permissions.

In [Factorize](https://app.factorize.sh), review access in **Clients**
and approved services in **Integrations**. You can change or revoke client
access there. You do not need to paste a service credential into MCP.

## Built-in workflow skills

Use `skills/list` to discover `use-an-api`, `grant-vm-access`, and
`manage-triggers`. Use `skills/get` for the returned manifest, then read its
advertised resource URI. Rediscover the catalog after an update rather than
pinning an old versioned URI. Clients that do not expose these methods can
follow the [same recipes](https://docs.factorize.sh/quickstart) in this guide.

See [MCP tools](https://docs.factorize.sh/mcp/tools) for the registered inventory and
[REST reference](https://docs.factorize.sh/api/reference) for the generated OpenAPI contract.

## Use a connected API
Source: https://docs.factorize.sh/work/use-an-api

Human setup: follow [Use an API](https://docs.factorize.sh/quickstart#use-an-api). Use a disposable
project or a test API; do not guess which production resources to query.

1. Call `get_api_reflection`. Choose an integration whose access is
   `granted` and use its ID and request example. Reflection is discovery,
   not authorization to call an integration marked `requestable` or
   `unavailable`. For an OAuth client, API calls require `proxy:use` and
   applicable integration access. When the connection needs an explicit
   integration scope, use the exact scope reported by Factorize; ask the
   human to review consent rather than requesting unrelated permissions.
2. Call `request_api` with `integration`, `method`, and an integration-relative
   `path`. Use a request that the provider documents as read-only; some
   providers use a POST for a read (GraphQL, for example). Never attach
   a provider authorization header or paste credentials into a tool call.
3. For a queued operation, poll `get_api_operation`; polling does not repeat
   the call. If the response is retained, read only what you need with
   `query_api_response` or `read_api_response`. Distinguish provider HTTP
   status from the Factorize operation completing.

For an isolated fixture, reflect a test integration pointing to a mock
service that returns `{"hello":"factorize"}` from `GET /sample`. Substitute
the integration ID actually returned by reflection:

```json request_api
{"integration":"11111111-1111-4111-8111-111111111111","method":"GET","path":"/sample","execution":"sync"}
```

Expect HTTP 200 and the fixture's message. Do not delete anything at the
provider. Have the owner remove temporary client or integration access if it
is no longer needed. See [MCP tools](https://docs.factorize.sh/mcp/tools#integration-apis) or the
[REST contract](https://docs.factorize.sh/api/reference).

## Give a VM access
Source: https://docs.factorize.sh/work/vm-access

Human setup: follow [Give a VM access](https://docs.factorize.sh/quickstart#give-a-vm-access).
Use a disposable running Fly.io Machine, not a shared workload, and confirm
its team and exact identity. Factorize supports VM grants for Fly.io Machines.
Exe.dev provider-native integration bindings are separate, not Factorize VM grants.

1. The authorizing client needs `vms:edit` to grant or revoke and `vms:read`
   to check its grants. It must also have the scopes it delegates. Some tools
   that discover provider connections additionally need `integrations:read`.
   Use the authorized provider connection's ID, not a provider credential.
2. Call `grant_vm_permissions` with a stable enrollment request key, the
   existing Machine target, and explicit `permissions.scopes`: only `triggers:read` here. This example
   is an isolated Fly.io fixture; substitute the actual provider connection,
   Machine ID, and app name. Use the live tool schema for other target fields.
3. From inside the test VM, authenticate using the returned audience, the
   provider's identity proof, and the enrolled guest key. See [VM
   authentication](https://docs.factorize.sh/mcp/tools#authenticate-from-an-enrolled-machine) for the
   signed Fly.io example. Do not copy the private key out of the guest or
   substitute the human's token. Call `list_events` from the VM or
   `GET /api/v1/events`; an empty list is valid. Use `list_vms` from the
   authorizing client to confirm the exact grant.
4. Call `revoke_vm_permissions` with that grant ID and check that it no longer
   appears in the active list. This does not stop or delete the VM.

```json grant_vm_permissions
{"target":{"kind":"machine","providerId":"11111111-1111-4111-8111-111111111111","vm":"1234abcd","app":"factorize-test","requestKey":"hello-factorize-v1"},"permissions":{"scopes":["triggers:read"]}}
```

To edit rather than enroll, use target `kind: "existing"`, the grant ID, and
`expectedRevision` from `list_vms`. Do not add provider APIs to a VM grant
unless the owner also approves the required API and integration scopes.
See [MCP tools](https://docs.factorize.sh/mcp/tools#vm-permissions) and [REST reference](https://docs.factorize.sh/api/reference).

## React to an Event
Source: https://docs.factorize.sh/work/triggers

Human setup: follow [React to an event](https://docs.factorize.sh/quickstart#react-to-an-event).
Use `triggers:write` for setup, manual fire, and cleanup; use
`triggers:read` for discovery, subscriptions, and reads.

1. In a test team use `create_event` with a unique test name and an object
   schema. Use the returned Event UUID as `eventId` in `create_trigger`.
   Add a manual source to start; no provider credential is needed.
2. If your client supports subscriptions, subscribe to
   `factorize://events/{eventId}/occurrences` before firing. Call
   `fire_trigger` with the returned Trigger ID, a stable `idempotencyKey`,
   and a message that matches the schema.
3. Use `list_event_occurrences` to verify the durable record (and to recover
   after a missed notification). Reuse the key for the same logical fire:
   it must not create another occurrence. Unsubscribe and use `delete_event`
   only for the confirmed test Event; deletion cascades to its Triggers
   and occurrence history.

```json create_event
{"name":"hello.factorize","payloadSchema":{"type":"object","properties":{"message":{"type":"string"}},"required":["message"]}}
```

```json create_trigger
{"eventId":"11111111-1111-4111-8111-111111111111","name":"hello-manual","sources":[{"kind":"manual"}]}
```

```json fire_trigger
{"triggerId":"22222222-2222-4222-8222-222222222222","idempotencyKey":"hello-factorize-1","data":{"message":"hello"}}
```

## What each signal means

- **Occurrence:** A validated Event record was committed. One Event can have
  several Triggers. It is not proof an agent ran.
- **Transport receipt:** A resource update tells a client to read; an HTTP
  callback receipt means a delivery endpoint accepted the request. Neither
  proves the subscriber finished processing.
- **Processing ACK:** An optional confirmation by the subscriber, recording
  durable completion or handoff on its exact subscription and original
  occurrence ID. It is not inferred from HTTP success.
- **Execution:** What the subscriber chooses to do. Factorize does not run
  an agent simply because it published an occurrence.

## Add a real input when ready

Use a [webhook or provider source](https://docs.factorize.sh/integrations/events), or select a schedule
with a cron expression and time zone. Work with recorded test evidence first.
Read the existing Trigger with `get_trigger` before replacing a configuration
with `update_trigger`. Inspect [delivery and ACK diagnostics](https://docs.factorize.sh/mcp/tools#optional-processing-acknowledgments)
rather than repeating a live action just to verify it.

Optional [Event enrichment](https://docs.factorize.sh/mcp/tools#opt-in-event-enrichment) maps different
Trigger sources into a common input, evaluates ordered named lookups using
existing authorized integrations, and applies one final Event-level rule.
Configure it with an OAuth grant authorized for `triggers:write`,
`proxy:use`, and every selected integration. Do not add live lookups to a test
Event. Lookups are not retried; safe evaluation results can be read through
`list_event_evaluations`, but raw provider response bodies are not stored or
delivered. The app shows attached Triggers and read-only match logic.

## AWS
Source: https://docs.factorize.sh/integrations/aws

AWS Code Mode runs Python on the AWS-hosted MCP server. Factorize authenticates and forwards the request; it does not run the code or keep an AWS action catalog. Make a separate, named Factorize connection for each AWS role or account. The caller selects a connection, not a role ARN.

## Connect an AWS account

1. Open **Settings → Integrations → Add AWS integration**. Name the connection and choose the Region for its AWS MCP endpoint.
2. Download the CloudFormation template. Upload it as a new stack in the target AWS account and acknowledge that it creates IAM resources. If that account already has an OIDC provider for this Factorize issuer, set `CreateProvider` to `false`.
3. Copy the stack's **RoleArn** output to Factorize and click **Verify AWS role**. The Worker assumes the role and signs a harmless Code Mode probe. This verifies the connection, not the full set of API permissions.
4. Optionally give one active Factorize OAuth connection **Use access** and save. That grant applies only to this AWS connection and this exact OAuth installation. Select **No Use access** to revoke it. AWS connections do not appear in workspace defaults or VM grants.

The agent calls `run_aws_script` with `connectionId` and `code`. It needs an active OAuth credential and the connection-specific Use grant, not `integrations:write` or any other additional Factorize scope. Only the owner, in an interactive session with `integrations:write`, can prepare, verify, delete or change access to the connection. It receives the script result and standard output, not authentication material or upstream session headers. The initial tool is request-scoped; Factorize does not poll background AWS tasks or replay timed-out requests. A timeout does not mean a script made no changes. Check AWS before retrying a modifying script.

## Trust and permissions

The starter role allows three inventory reads. Change the IAM permissions for that role in AWS if a workflow needs more; there is no Factorize operation list to maintain. Prefer a different role and Factorize connection for workflows that can write. The Worker gets a 15-minute STS session and signs requests to the AWS MCP endpoint with SigV4. It does not pass credentials to the script. The session narrows the role to the AWS-hosted MCP path and excludes IAM administration, credential chaining, and interactive host access. AWS applies the customer's role, resource and organization policies to the actual calls.

Deleting the connection stops new requests from Factorize. Remove the role or its trust in AWS as well. The template retains the account-wide OIDC provider so it does not break other Factorize roles. Remove that provider separately when no roles use it.

## Deploying the issuer

Before enabling setup, configure the Worker secret `AWS_WORKLOAD_SIGNING_KEYS` with JSON containing `active` (a dedicated RSA private JWK with a unique `kid`) and optional `previous` (up to two public JWKs). Use 2048- or 3072-bit RSA. Do not reuse the browser OAuth signer. The Worker publishes discovery at `<app origin>/oauth/aws/.well-known/openid-configuration` and public keys at `<app origin>/oauth/aws/jwks`; no public endpoint issues workload tokens. Without a configured secret the integration fails closed.

For key rotation, first publish the new public key alongside the old active key and allow for AWS JWKS caching. Then switch the active signer and keep the old public key for the overlap. Never include a private key in the public key set or store it in source control.

## Event payloads and conditions
Source: https://docs.factorize.sh/integrations/events

An Event has a versioned JSON payload schema. Every Trigger attached to that
Event publishes an occurrence only when its resulting payload passes the current
schema. Stored occurrences keep their schema revision and payload.

Webhook Triggers can include conditions evaluated against prepared provider
context. The condition preview tool evaluates example data only; it does not
authenticate, route, or publish an occurrence. Repeated delivery IDs are
idempotent. Inspect safe outcomes with `list_trigger_webhook_activity` and
`list_webhook_deliveries`.

MCP subscribers receive resource update notifications after an occurrence is
stored. Notifications indicate that the resource changed; clients read the
resource or list occurrences to obtain durable data.

In the Factorize dashboard, open **Events** to see event definitions and their
subscriber counts. Select an Event to see its attached Triggers, match logic
when configured, occurrence history, and subscriptions. The **Subscriptions** sidebar shows registration
status and acknowledgment mode for your MCP connections in the current
workspace. The subscriber count includes active registrations only; an active
registration does not guarantee that the client can receive deliveries.

## GitHub Triggers
Source: https://docs.factorize.sh/integrations/github

Connect a GitHub installation, then attach a GitHub source Trigger to an Event.
Choose the installation, repository, webhook event, action, and optional
conditions in the Trigger configuration. Factorize verifies webhook signatures
and deduplicates provider delivery IDs before validating and storing the Event
occurrence.

Inspect safe delivery outcomes with `list_trigger_webhook_activity` and
`list_webhook_deliveries`. Use [Event payload and condition guidance](https://docs.factorize.sh/integrations/events)
for payload validation and [troubleshooting](https://docs.factorize.sh/troubleshooting/events) for
rejected or missing deliveries.

## ClickUp Triggers
Source: https://docs.factorize.sh/integrations/clickup

Connect ClickUp and attach a ClickUp source Trigger to an Event. Select the
workspace resources and match rules in the browser editor. Matching signed
webhook deliveries produce validated durable occurrences; duplicate delivery
IDs are ignored.

Inspect safe delivery outcomes with `list_trigger_webhook_activity` and
`list_webhook_deliveries`. See [Event payloads and conditions](https://docs.factorize.sh/integrations/events)
and [troubleshooting](https://docs.factorize.sh/troubleshooting/events).

## Integration access
Source: https://docs.factorize.sh/integrations/oauth

Integrations hold server-side credentials used to validate provider webhooks or
make authorized API requests. Select only the integrations needed for your
Triggers or MCP connection. Credentials are encrypted and never returned by
Factorize APIs.

Bearer API, GitHub, Linear, ClickUp, X, Fly.io, exe.dev, Amp, and Cloudflare REST API
integrations have distinct setup flows. Cloudflare Tail is retired. Use the browser's Integrations page to connect or revoke
credentials and to choose which MCP clients may access them.

Choose **Delete** on a supported integration to preview its impact, then confirm.
Deleting removes the connection from Factorize, not the provider. For Linear,
Factorize removes its saved OAuth connection and webhook routing for that
workspace. Affected Trigger sources, Event lookups, and client or workload
access are listed before confirmation. A Trigger with no sources left is
removed, but Event definitions, subscriptions, and recorded occurrences are
kept. Reconnecting does not restore removed configuration or grants.


### Hetzner Cloud

Add the project in **Integrations → Hetzner Cloud** with a Hetzner project
token. Check **Hetzner Cloud** in an OAuth client's permissions to allow it
to use the native API and its enrolled SSH access. Unchecking it removes
both immediately; neither change requires reconnecting the OAuth client.

Hetzner enforces the project token's permissions. Choose **Read** for inventory
only. With a **Read & Write** token, checked clients can make changes, delete
resources, and incur charges. The existing client checkboxes are unchanged
by this update: a client already checked for a project with a Read & Write
token can make writes immediately. Replacing the project still resets client
API grants and probe enrollments; reassign only clients that need API access.
Client SSH key pairs stay attached to the client, independent of the project.

Use `get_api_reflection` to find the authorized Hetzner connection ID. Then
use the standard `request_api` tool with the method, relative `/v1/...` path,
query, and JSON body described in the [Hetzner Cloud API](https://docs.hetzner.cloud/reference/cloud).
For example, list servers using `GET /v1/servers`. To create a server, use
Hetzner's native `POST /v1/servers` body. Factorize does not rewrite it or
return the project token. Hetzner enforces the token's access. As with other
proxy connections, OAuth also needs `proxy:use`; Hetzner's checkbox controls
access to the specific project and is rechecked before dispatch and before
retained results can be read. The proxy defaults to asynchronous execution.
Use a stable `idempotencyKey` for a write and inspect the operation instead of
repeating an uncertain request.

#### Factorize SSH key management

`get_hetzner_ssh_public_key` returns the calling OAuth installation's public
key and a restricted authorized-keys line. Private keys are encrypted and
not exposed. Owners and their authorized clients can use Hetzner's native
SSH-key API through the proxy. A Hetzner project SSH-key record by itself
does not install a key on an existing server. During native server creation,
Hetzner's `ssh_keys` field places keys according to the selected image's
defaults. To use Factorize's authentication check, configure the complete
restricted key line on a dedicated non-root account, then independently
obtain the host's Ed25519 fingerprint from a trusted console. In **View
servers**, the owner enrolls that account, selects the exact OAuth client,
and sets the trusted fingerprint. Existing enrollments created by Factorize's
former server tool retain their original client binding.

`check_hetzner_ssh` revalidates project membership and the pinned public IPv4
for the client's enrolled server, proves fresh authentication with the
pinned host key, and closes immediately. It never starts a shell, runs
commands, or returns output. Remove the installed public key on the server
when retiring access; removing a connection in Factorize does not change
the server.


### Run commands over SSH

The SSH server decides whether a client can log in. Ask the connected client
to call `get_ssh_public_key`; add that public key to the account it should use.
For a new Hetzner server, use the native Hetzner API through `request_api`.
Use a dedicated non-root account and discover its host fingerprint through a
trusted provider console. An owner then saves the public IP, username, and
fingerprint using `POST /api/v1/ssh/targets` from an authenticated owner session,
and supplies the returned target ID to the client. No private key is exposed.

`ssh_exec` takes that target ID and one command. It returns stdout, stderr
and the exit code, with a truncation flag if output exceeded the response
limit. Commands do not share a shell, working directory, or environment.
The broker can reuse the authenticated connection for up to 30 seconds
idle and no more than two minutes in total. A timed-out command may still
have run; do not retry without reconciling its effects.

For a Hetzner Cloud server, list the project inventory through `request_api`
or open **View servers** in Factorize. Call `ssh_exec` with `hetznerServerId`
instead of `targetId`. Install the client's public key on a non-root account
first. Factorize uses the saved username, or `factorize-agent` if none is
saved; use the optional `username` argument to choose another account.

Factorize looks up the current address through the connected Hetzner project
and saves the Ed25519 host fingerprint after the first successful SSH login,
before executing a command. This is trust on first use, not independent
verification of the initial fingerprint. To verify it out of band, save it
in **SSH commands** before connecting. A changed fingerprint blocks execution
until an owner verifies and saves the replacement. Generic `targetId` targets
still require a fingerprint before the first connection.

The Hetzner checkbox governs provider access, including the server-ID lookup.
It does not install or remove authorized keys on the server and does not
govern generic targets selected by `targetId`. Removing an authorized key on the server denies fresh
SSH connections; terminate the existing connection on the server too if
revocation must be immediate. Previously installed probe-only keys remain
probe-only unless the server operator changes the authorization.

## Connection problems
Source: https://docs.factorize.sh/troubleshooting/connection

| Symptom | Action |
| --- | --- |
| Browser consent fails or is cancelled | Sign in to the intended Factorize account, restart authorization from the client, and approve the requested scopes. |
| The authorization link expired or was used | Start **Reconnect** in the MCP client and open its new authorization link. Keep approval in the same browser and Factorize account. If only the consent form expired, reload it and review the choices again. |
| Saved permissions are missing from consent | Save the scopes in **Clients**, then start **Reconnect** from the MCP client. In Factorize, select the same existing connection. Available saved scopes are offered separately even when the client initially asks for fewer. The new token reports its scopes; an old access or refresh credential does not gain permissions. |
| Client never connects | Confirm `https://app.factorize.sh/mcp`, remote Streamable HTTP and OAuth support. Open the client's MCP status view and authenticate; see [connection guide](https://docs.factorize.sh/mcp/overview). |
| `invalid_token` or access disappears | Reauthorize the client. A password reset or changing account security can invalidate delegated credentials. Browser sign-out alone does not revoke the client. |
| `insufficient_scope` | Reconnect and grant `triggers:read` to discover Events and occurrences, or `triggers:write` to manage Events and Triggers. Add integration scopes only when needed. |
| Provider input is not arriving | Check the saved integration and Trigger source configuration. For delivery diagnosis, see [Event troubleshooting](https://docs.factorize.sh/troubleshooting/events). |

Revoking an MCP authorization affects access but does not delete stored Events,
Triggers, or occurrences. Provider reconnection is separate and can be managed
from the Integrations page.

## Event and Trigger troubleshooting
Source: https://docs.factorize.sh/troubleshooting/events

## No occurrence was created

1. Confirm that the Trigger is enabled and belongs to the intended Event.
2. Inspect its source configuration and integration connection in the browser.
3. For a webhook, inspect `list_trigger_webhook_activity` and
   `list_webhook_deliveries` for signature, condition, routing, or duplicate
   outcomes. These records omit secrets and raw payloads.
4. Check that the Event's current payload schema accepts the resulting JSON.
5. For manual firing, confirm the Trigger kind and reuse the original
   idempotency key when retrying an uncertain request.

## A subscriber missed a notification

Notifications tell the client that an Event resource changed; they are not the
stored payload. Read the Event resource or call `list_event_occurrences` to
recover durable occurrences after reconnecting. Confirm the client has
`triggers:read` and supports MCP resource subscriptions.

## MCP tool reference
Source: https://docs.factorize.sh/mcp/tools

Connect to `https://app.factorize.sh/mcp` using [client authorization](https://docs.factorize.sh/mcp/overview).
Tools return structured JSON. IDs must come from the authorized workspace.

## Inventory

Every tool listed below is registered by the MCP server. The server validates
its input and enforces the operation's required scope.

| Tool | Description from MCP discovery |
| --- | --- |
| `acknowledge_events` | After durable completion or handoff, acknowledge exact original data.occurrenceId UUIDs on your opted-in subscription. Never pass a recovery wake ID or assume an ordered range. Ack successful work promptly; optional cooldown applies only when a new ID is acknowledged, not on retries. Keep client-local pacing and don't drop unfinished work. |
| `append_payload_chunk` | Append a small generated UTF8/base64 chunk at the returned payload byte size. Identical retries are safe. |
| `cancel_api_operation` | Cancel an HTTP operation. Upstream writes may already have taken effect. |
| `check_hetzner_ssh` | Check SSH access for one owner-enrolled Hetzner Cloud server. Uses the pinned host identity and a Factorize-held credential. Proves fresh key authentication; no SSH channel, commands or remote output. |
| `create_app` | Register a server-side app. Create client secrets separately in the browser. |
| `create_event` | Create a durable Event that one or more Triggers can publish. |
| `create_payload` | Reserve a temporary request body. Open browserUploadUrl to upload an existing file for that connection, or append/finalize generated text in chunks. Pass the finalized handle to request_api bodySource. |
| `create_trigger` | Create an input Trigger attached to an Event. Credentials are never accepted or returned. |
| `delete_event` | Permanently delete an Event, all its Triggers and input configurations, and its occurrence history. |
| `delete_trigger` | Delete an input Trigger |
| `disable_trigger` | Disable a trigger |
| `enable_trigger` | Enable a trigger |
| `fetch_payload` | Import unchanged file bytes from an authorized integration into a temporary request payload. |
| `finalize_payload` | Finalize an immutable request payload; optional SHA256 verifies exact bytes. |
| `fire_trigger` | Fire an enabled Trigger and persist an Event occurrence. Reuse idempotencyKey to make retries safe. |
| `get_api_operation` | Poll a durable HTTP operation. Does not repeat the upstream request. |
| `get_api_reflection` | Use this first to discover authorized integration APIs and request_api examples. Call request_api with the returned integration ID; no shell or raw credential is needed. Availability is not a credential health check. |
| `get_app` | Read a registered app's non-secret metadata. |
| `get_event` | Read an Event and its current payload schema revision. |
| `get_event_processing_acknowledgments` | Read optional processing acknowledgment settings for your exact active MCP subscription. Off by default; independent of HTTP receipt and client-side throttling. |
| `get_hetzner_ssh_public_key` | Get this authorized OAuth installation’s public SSH key. The owner must install it on existing servers; the private key is never returned. |
| `get_ssh_public_key` | Get the public SSH key of this saved Factorize client. Install it on a server account to grant that key access. The private key is never returned. |
| `get_trigger` | Get a Trigger, its parent Event, and input configuration |
| `get_webhook_delivery` | Get a webhook delivery and its safe processing timeline. Secrets and payloads are never returned. |
| `grant_vm_permissions` | Grant or replace Factorize permissions for an existing VM. Use explicit scopes within your effective access. Requires vms:edit. |
| `import_attachment` | Import a user-attached ChatGPT file directly into temporary artifact storage. Returns a payload handle for request_api. Missing native download URLs require create_payload and its browserUploadUrl. |
| `list_apps` | List the team's registered server-side apps. Requires apps:manage. |
| `list_cloudflare_tail_integrations` | Legacy; historical installations only. List installed Cloudflare Tail integrations and reference counts. Signing secrets are never returned. |
| `list_event_evaluations` | Read recent Event evaluation diagnostics and mapped input, without raw lookup responses. |
| `list_event_occurrences` | Read durable Event occurrences in reverse recorded order, not UUID order. Reads do not acknowledge processing or define a task batch. |
| `list_events` | List Events, their current payload schema revisions, and Trigger and occurrence counts. |
| `list_exe_connections` | List safe metadata for saved exe.dev connections. API tokens are never returned. |
| `list_github_installations` | List connected GitHub App installations, including the installation IDs needed by GitHub Trigger events. Credentials are never returned. |
| `list_trigger_webhook_activity` | List matching, rejected, duplicate, and accepted webhook activity for a trigger |
| `list_triggers` | List triggers and their parent Events |
| `list_vms` | List active Factorize permission grants for team VMs. Requires vms:read. |
| `list_webhook_deliveries` | Search tenant-scoped webhook deliveries by provider, delivery ID, event, outcome, trigger, time range, or safe diagnostic text. Results are newest first and cursor paginated. |
| `query_api_response` | Query a retained response without loading it into context. JSON supports bounded JMESPath fields/projections/filters, text uses line offsets, bytes uses byte offsets. Parsing is limited to 1 MiB; use byte ranges for larger bodies. |
| `read_api_operation` | Read bounded incremental response bytes, including partial bytes after failure. Poll get_api_operation for status. |
| `read_api_response` | Read a retained integration response chunk with the same authorization as the original request. |
| `read_event_delivery_diagnostics` | Read separate safe HTTP and optional processing diagnostics for one original occurrence ID. A 2xx receipt is not acknowledgment. Does not return payloads or callback details or retry deliveries. |
| `read_event_occurrences` | Read committed Event payloads by occurrenceId or by definitionId and an inclusive recorded-time since value. Follow nextCursor with the same definitionId and since. Read recovery wakes by original data.occurrenceId, not their fresh eventId. Reads do not consume history or acknowledge processing; handle out-of-order work by exact ID. |
| `rename_mcp_client` | Set the display name of this OAuth connection in Authorized clients. |
| `replay_unacknowledged_events` | Queue exact unresolved original occurrence IDs on your opted-in subscription, without duplicating business events or bypassing cooldown. Recovery wakes can have fresh event IDs; deduplicate by their original data.occurrenceId. |
| `request_api` | Call an integration discovered by get_api_reflection. Use its integration ID and relative path; no VM, shell or credential is needed. Credentials stay in Factorize. OAuth requires proxy:use. Use read_api_response for retained response handles. |
| `revoke_vm_permissions` | Revoke a VM's Factorize permissions. The VM keeps running. Requires vms:edit. |
| `run_aws_script` | Run Python in the AWS-hosted MCP sandbox through an AWS connection whose owner granted this OAuth installation Use access. The customer role controls AWS API permissions; permitted writes can change resources and incur charges. Never assume a retry after timeout is safe. |
| `set_event_processing_acknowledgments` | Opt in to processing acknowledgments for future occurrences on your exact MCP subscription. Turning off waives unresolved acknowledgments and clears cooldown; does not alter standard MCP subscription behavior. |
| `ssh_exec` | Run one non-interactive SSH command. Supply a saved targetId or a hetznerServerId from the native Hetzner server list. For Hetzner, Factorize saves the Ed25519 host fingerprint after the first successful login and blocks changes. Set username to a non-root account with the client key installed (default: factorize-agent or the saved username). The server decides if this client's key is authorized. Each call opens a fresh command channel, possibly on a warm connection. Do not retry a timed-out command blindly. |
| `test_trigger_webhook_conditions` | Evaluate conditions on supplied prepared webhook context. No authentication of the example, routing, live GitHub verification, or Trigger firing. |
| `update_app` | Update redirect URLs, visibility, or enabled state for a registered app. |
| `update_event` | Create a new Event payload schema revision; existing occurrences retain their original revision. |
| `update_trigger` | Replace a Trigger's input configuration and Event parent. |

## Events and occurrences

`list_events` and `get_event` discover Event definitions and their payload
schemas. `create_event` and `update_event` manage those definitions. Each Event
may have multiple Triggers. An enabled Trigger publishes an occurrence only
after validating the payload against the Event's current JSON schema.

Subscribe to `factorize://events/{eventId}/occurrences` using MCP resource
subscription support. After a resource-updated notification, read the resource
to retrieve durable data. `list_event_occurrences` lets a reconnecting client
recover stored records.

MCP Events clients discover the stable `factorize.occurrence` type with
`events/list` and subscribe using `arguments: { "event_id": "<uuid>" }`.
Get the UUID from `create_event` or `list_events`; no plugin refresh is
needed for new Event definitions after the one-time catalog refresh. Reuse the
same name, arguments, and callback to renew or unsubscribe. Existing per-Event
subscriptions keep their original names and continue receiving webhooks.
Each notification includes the occurrence and definition IDs. Call
`read_event_occurrences` with `occurrenceId` for the committed payload. For a
wake without an ID, call it with the saved `definitionId` and a recent `since`
time, and follow `nextCursor` with the same definition and time. Windowed reads
use recorded time so recent arrivals with older source timestamps appear.
Reads leave history intact.

Use `read_event_delivery_diagnostics` with an exact `occurrenceId` to
inspect outbound MCP webhook delivery. `no_delivery_records` means the
occurrence exists but no delivery rows are recorded; a missing occurrence
returns not found. Rows distinguish pending/sending, accepted, failed, and
cancelled delivery. They show opaque subscription IDs, attempt counts, safe outcome codes, HTTP status,
and timestamps, never payloads or callback details. Callback acceptance is
not proof that a downstream task ran. This is separate from inbound webhook
delivery tools and cannot retry an outbound message.


`delete_event` permanently removes the Event, all attached Triggers and input
configurations, and all stored occurrences.

### Optional processing acknowledgments

The standard MCP subscription request and HTTP delivery behavior are unchanged.
HTTP 2xx means the callback accepted the wake, not that a task ran. Opt in for
future occurrences on the exact subscription using
`set_event_processing_acknowledgments` after subscribing. The setting is off
by default. The same active OAuth grant with `triggers:read` can read it with
`get_event_processing_acknowledgments`.

- Acknowledge promptly **after** durable processing or handoff. Call
  `acknowledge_events` with the exact `subscription_id` and successful original
  `event_ids` from `data.occurrenceId`. Arrays accept 1–100 UUIDs. An ACK
  reports newly processed, already processed, and not acknowledged IDs; do not
  treat the last group as completed work.
- A wake may arrive out of order or contain only part of the work. A recovery
  webhook may use a fresh top-level `eventId`; read and deduplicate by the
  unchanged original `data.occurrenceId`. UUIDs do not imply ordering or a
  high-water mark. Do not assume a platform batch window, run cap, or check
  cadence. Page durable history by its documented cursor and retain any work
  you cannot complete; do not silently drop it.
- To rate limit, pace in your client first. An optional `cooldown_seconds`
  (1–3600) on an ACK with newly completed work pauses delivery only on that
  subscription. Retrying the same ACK does not extend cooldown. Delayed
  delivery remains durable and resumes when cooldown expires even without a
  new event.
- If the ACK timeout expires, Factorize sends bounded recovery wakes for that
  original occurrence. Use `read_event_delivery_diagnostics` to distinguish HTTP
  acceptance from awaiting ACK, processed, waived, cancelled, and exhausted.
  `replay_unacknowledged_events` queues exact unresolved IDs on your active
  opted-in subscription, subject to cooldown; it does not create business
  occurrences or replay completed work.
- Turning off waives unresolved acknowledgments, cancels unstarted recovery,
  and clears subscription cooldown. Turning it on again applies only to
  future occurrences. A reactivated subscription is a fresh generation and
  starts with acknowledgments off.


## Triggers

A Trigger belongs to one Event and watches a schedule, signed webhook/provider
input, or manual fire request. Duplicate deliveries are deduplicated. Reuse the
same `idempotencyKey` after an uncertain manual fire. Webhook activity tools
show safe processing outcomes without exposing secrets or raw payloads.

`create_trigger` and `update_trigger` require a parent `eventId` and an
explicit `sources` array of input configurations. For a manual-only Trigger,
send `sources: [{ "kind": "manual" }]`. Read a Trigger before replacing its
configuration.

## Integration APIs

Integration tools use server-held credentials and current authorization; credentials are never
returned. `get_api_reflection` describes available integrations and safe request
examples before `request_api` is used. See [REST reference](https://docs.factorize.sh/api/reference) for
exact request and response schemas.

## VM permissions

Use `grant_vm_permissions` to enroll an existing Machine through a team VM
provider connection. Supply the team's integration ID as `providerId`, the
Machine ID as `vm`, and the Fly app name as `app`. Create a request key once and
reuse it for retries. Initial enrollment requires a running Machine with
`curl`, `openssl`, and permission to use the Fly OIDC socket in the guest.

```json
{
  "target": {
    "kind": "machine",
    "providerId": "9dd924e0-3a35-48d5-bcd1-56e4b0922265",
    "vm": "1234abcd",
    "app": "my-app",
    "requestKey": "my-app-workload-1"
  },
  "permissions": { "scopes": ["triggers:read"] }
}
```

Provide explicit `permissions.scopes` for the grant. Factorize saves a scope
snapshot and rejects the entire request if any requested scope is outside the
caller's effective access. To replace permissions, supply a `target` with
`kind: "existing"`, `grantId`, and `expectedRevision` from `list_vms`. Revoking
a grant removes its Factorize permissions while the workload keeps running.
Enrollment is available only for providers enabled after identity validation.

### Authenticate from an enrolled Machine

On Fly.io, request an OIDC token through the `/.fly/api` Unix socket. POST
`{"aud":"<grant authentication.audience>"}` to `http://localhost/v1/tokens/oidc`.
Keep the private key in the guest at the returned `authentication.guestKeyPath`,
relative to the enrollment user's home directory.

For each REST or MCP HTTP request, set these headers:

- `Authorization: Bearer <provider OIDC token>`
- `X-Factorize-VM-Grant: <grant ID>`
- `X-Factorize-VM-Proof: <signed proof JWT>`

Sign the proof with the enrolled P-256 private key. Use JWT header fields
`alg: "ES256"` and `typ: "factorize-vm-proof+jwt"`, and encode the signature in
the 64-byte JWS format. Include these claims:

| Claim | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `grant` | Grant ID |
| `ath` | Unpadded base64url SHA-256 of the provider token |
| `htm` | HTTP method |
| `htu` | Absolute request URL, including its query string |
| `jti` | A new UUID for each HTTP request |
| `iat` | Current Unix time in seconds |

Send the proof within 60 seconds and sign a fresh proof for every retry. MCP
workloads need a transport that can set dynamic HTTP headers. The VM uses
the scopes in its saved grant and refreshes its provider token before expiry.

## Opt-in Event enrichment

An Event can define an ordered `enrichment.extraDataUrls` list and one boolean
JMESPath `rule`. A Trigger attached to it supplies an `inputMapping` from dotted
paths in its evidence to common, scalar input keys. Usual Trigger prefilters
run first. Each lookup uses a fixed integration and HTTP method. Its path is
relative to that integration; Mustache variables can reference `input.name`
or an earlier `lookups.step.field`. Path values are single safe segments and
query values are escaped as data. Credentials come only from the authorized
integration. Configure and edit an enriched Trigger using an OAuth grant with
the explicit matching integration scopes, `proxy:use`, and `triggers:write`.

The final rule sees the normalized `input` and `lookups`. No lookup response
bodies are persisted, shown on the Event page, or delivered. Only mapped input
becomes the occurrence payload; choose those fields deliberately. Diagnostics
are available through `list_event_evaluations` or the authenticated
`GET /api/v1/events/{eventId}/evaluations` endpoint. They include named step
results, a safe failure reason, and mapped input, not raw provider responses.
Missing inputs, failed lookups, revoked access, and interrupted attempts stop
evaluation without retrying or creating an occurrence.

## Events and Triggers
Source: https://docs.factorize.sh/concepts

A **team** owns Events, Triggers, integrations, and authorization settings.

An **Event** is a named durable record with a versioned JSON payload schema. A
matching Trigger creates an occurrence, which subscribers can read later. An
Event may have multiple Triggers.

A **Trigger** watches one input source: a schedule, signed webhook, provider
notification, or explicit fire request. Matching and duplicate-delivery checks
happen before Factorize validates and stores the Event occurrence. A Trigger
publishes data; it does not launch an agent or create an execution.

MCP clients discover Event definitions, subscribe to their occurrence resource,
and receive a resource-updated notification after a new occurrence. They then
read the resource to obtain durable data. Occurrences are also available through
the authorized REST API, so a reconnecting client can recover stored data.

## REST API reference
Source: https://docs.factorize.sh/api/reference

The **REST operations** group under Reference renders every application operation directly from [openapi.yaml](https://docs.factorize.sh/openapi.yaml), including request validation, required scopes, owner-session restrictions, and JSON response schemas. This is the same generated artifact verified by CI and available to API clients.

All application endpoints use `/api/v1`. Authenticate with a scoped bearer token or an interactive owner session; credential management and trace replay require an interactive owner session. Errors use `{ "error": { "code": "...", "message": "..." } }`.

`GET /healthz` is the unauthenticated infrastructure liveness probe and returns `{ "ok": true }`. It is outside the application API contract.

See [authentication](https://docs.factorize.sh/api/authentication) for access setup and [OpenAPI definition](https://docs.factorize.sh/api/openapi) for downloading or regenerating the contract.

## Authentication and scopes
Source: https://docs.factorize.sh/api/authentication

Protected REST and MCP requests use `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. Browser
users may also use their signed Factorize session cookie. Access is tenant-bound;
ownership and session version are rechecked on service calls.

## Scopes

| Scope | Allows |
| --- | --- |
| `team:read` | Read team settings |
| `team:write` | Update team settings |
| `triggers:read` | Discover Events, Triggers, and stored occurrences |
| `triggers:write` | Manage Events and Triggers |
| `integrations:read` | Read integration metadata and provider resources |
| `integrations:write` | Manage integration connections |
| `proxy:use` | Use authorized external integration APIs |
| `apps:manage` | Manage registered applications |

Scopes are independent; write does not imply read. Integration-specific scopes
are granted separately. Owner-only operations require an interactive browser
session.

Owners can edit the saved permissions for an existing MCP connection in
Settings. Removals restrict access immediately; adding scopes requires fresh
authorization and never increases a previously issued token's scope.
Workspace permissions marked Default are preselected for new browser
connections. They do not change existing grants. Reconnecting shows the
saved selection and distinguishes newly requested permissions; the client
must include all scopes it wants to retain or add when requesting step-up.

## OAuth clients

Authorization-code clients must use PKCE S256. Implicit and plain PKCE are
disabled. Access tokens last one hour; refresh tokens can last up to 30 days.
RFC 7009 revocation is advertised by discovery. Device authorization is also
supported for public clients; follow the advertised OAuth metadata and device
verification instructions.

Never send provider credentials to an API client. Stored integration secrets
are used server-side and omitted from responses.

## OAuth discovery
Source: https://docs.factorize.sh/api/discovery

At `https://app.factorize.sh`, clients can retrieve:

* `/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server` — issuer, authorization, token, registration, revocation, and device endpoints plus supported grants/scopes.
* `/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource` — resource `https://app.factorize.sh/mcp`, authorization server, header bearer authentication, and supported scopes.

The authorization endpoint is `/authorize`, token endpoint `/oauth/token`, dynamic registration endpoint `/oauth/register`, and device endpoint `/oauth/device_authorization`. Client ID Metadata Documents are enabled. MCP clients should use `https://app.factorize.sh/mcp`; they can discover OAuth automatically and complete browser PKCE consent.

## OpenAPI definition
Source: https://docs.factorize.sh/api/openapi

[Download openapi.yaml](https://docs.factorize.sh/openapi.yaml). Clients can use this exact file to generate SDKs or inspect request and response schemas.

The definition is generated from the capability route declarations assembled by `packages/api/src/api-contract.ts`. For an API change, update the owning capability’s `api/rest.ts` declaration (method, path, scope, validation, handler, and documentation), then run:

```bash
npm run generate:openapi
```

Commit `packages/docs/openapi.yaml` with the change. CI regenerates it and rejects a diff; parsed contract tests also require exact method/path equality with the executable catalog. Shared schemas and general API metadata live beside the catalog in `trigger-schemas.ts`, `trace-replay-schemas.ts`, and `api-document.json`.

Run `npm run validate --workspace=factorize-docs` to verify the generated artifact, parsed operation contract, and Mintlify configuration before publishing.

## REST operations
Contract: https://docs.factorize.sh/openapi.yaml
The site renders this exact generated contract under Reference → REST operations.

## Optional self-hosting
Source: https://docs.factorize.sh/self-hosting/deployment

Hosted users can start at [app.factorize.sh](https://app.factorize.sh) without deploying anything. Self-hosting is for operators who want to own the application infrastructure.

The Worker lives in `packages/api`, React frontend in `packages/app`, and generated public client in `packages/api-client`. Use Node 24 and the root lockfile. Follow the [API-first deployment and rollback gates](https://github.com/GenerationSoftware/factorize/blob/main/docs/package-migration.md) before deploying static assets. Preserve Worker identity, bindings, migrations, and old hashed assets.

Install dependencies with `npm ci`. Configure `packages/api/wrangler.jsonc`, PostgreSQL, OAuth KV and artifact storage, set the final HTTPS `APP_ORIGIN`, then build with `npm run build:app` and deploy with `npm run deploy:app`. See [configuration](https://docs.factorize.sh/self-hosting/configuration) before deployment.

For local development, copy `packages/api/.dev.vars.example` to `packages/api/.dev.vars`, supply local configuration, and use `npm run dev`. Development uses HTTPS at `https://localhost:5173`; use that origin for local callbacks. The migration guide covers local database setup. Never commit secrets.

## Operator configuration
Source: https://docs.factorize.sh/self-hosting/configuration

These steps apply only to your own deployment. Hosted Factorize users connect existing accounts in [Integrations](https://app.factorize.sh/integrations); they do not register Factorize OAuth applications or set Worker secrets.

Register provider applications for your deployment origin. Linear requires Issues and Issue labels webhooks and fresh workspace authorization after subscription changes; ClickUp registers its task webhook on connection. Configure the GitHub App credentials and webhook settings for your deployment using the template in `packages/api/.dev.vars.example` and the executable callbacks/webhook routes in `packages/api/src/worker.ts`.

## Account authentication

Factorize owns authentication in PostgreSQL. Create a native account at `/auth/signup` with an email address and a password of 12–200 characters. Emails are case-insensitive. Verify the email before signing in at `/auth/login`; email plus password are accepted. Linear is connected after sign-in from **Integrations**, only for Linear-backed triggers.

Postmark sends one-hour, single-use verification and password-reset links. `/auth/verify/request` resends verification; `/auth/password-reset` handles recovery. Links never appear in application responses or logs. Passwords use salted PBKDF2-SHA-256. **Change password** in the account menu requires the current password. Password reset, password change and sign-out invalidate existing sessions via membership session versions, including delegated API credentials.

Before deploying, configure `POSTMARK_SERVER_TOKEN` as a **production GitHub environment secret**. The deployment copies it to a Worker secret; the verified sender and transactional message stream are non-secret Worker vars in `packages/api/wrangler.jsonc`. For a manual Postmark preflight, set the following environment variables along with `APP_ORIGIN`:

| Setting | Required value |
| --- | --- |
| `POSTMARK_SERVER_TOKEN` | Postmark **server** API token for the sending server; never an account token or a committed value |
| `POSTMARK_FROM_EMAIL` | Plain email address on a verified Postmark sender signature or verified domain |
| `POSTMARK_MESSAGE_STREAM` | Active **transactional** stream ID, commonly `outbound` |

`APP_ORIGIN` must be the canonical HTTPS origin, without a trailing slash. Run `npm run auth:validate-email --workspace=factorize` manually when needed: it checks the server token/stream with Postmark and sends one preflight email from/to the configured sender, rejecting unverified senders or sending failures. It prints no credentials. Missing configuration fails the manual check. The deploy workflow does not run this check or send a preflight email. Runtime signup and recovery also fail closed if configuration or delivery fails; users can resend verification after a delivery failure. Local mail testing needs an HTTPS origin and a separate Postmark test server/sender; automated tests mock Postmark and never send mail.

### Optional Google sign-in

Create a **Web application** OAuth client in Google Cloud. Register exactly
`<APP_ORIGIN>/oauth/google/sign-in/callback` as an authorized redirect URI
(`https://app.factorize.sh/oauth/google/sign-in/callback` on the hosted deployment).
Complete Google's OAuth consent screen setup for your intended audience. Set
`GOOGLE_SIGN_IN_CLIENT_ID` and `GOOGLE_SIGN_IN_CLIENT_SECRET` as Worker secrets.
The Google button is hidden unless both values are set. Apply migration 0104
using the normal database deployment step. Google sign-in is separate from
Factorize's MCP authorization clients and uses only `openid email`.

A first Google sign-in matching an existing verified Factorize account
requires its current Factorize password; email alone never links accounts.
New Google users choose a unique Factorize username. For addresses Google
does not manage directly, Factorize emails a confirmation link to be opened
in the browser that started signup. Once signed in, Google-first users can
use **Set password**. First confirm the linked Google account again, then open the
Factorize email link in that same browser. An email link alone cannot establish a
first password on a Google account.

Addresses verified independently by Factorize are not replaced by Google.
For accounts enrolled using Google's authoritative email, Google remains the
authority for password recovery even after a password is added. Factorize
retires the old email's recovery authority and outstanding links when a Google
address change is observed. If the new address needs independent confirmation,
prove it through the Google recovery flow. If it is already used by another
Factorize account, password recovery pauses rather than transferring or combining
accounts. Sign-in with the linked Google account still works. Keep Postmark
configured for address confirmation and password recovery.

### Optional two-factor authentication

Two-factor authentication is off by default and configured by each user in
**Account settings → Two-factor authentication**. There is no team enforcement.
Set `TOTP_ENCRYPTION_KEY` as an independent Worker secret before offering
enrollment. Generate 32 cryptographically random bytes encoded as base64 (for
example, using `openssl rand -base64 32`). Do not reuse the credential encryption
key or store the value in the repository. Normal deployment applies migration
0105. Keep the key securely backed up; changing it without re-encrypting
existing TOTP secrets breaks authenticator verification for enrolled users.
Users with a saved recovery code can still sign in.

Enrollment requires confirmation of the current Factorize password, or fresh
Google confirmation for Google-only users. The setup QR code is generated in
the browser without sending the secret to a QR service. Users confirm a valid
authenticator code to enable 2FA and should immediately save the ten recovery
codes, which are shown once and work once each. Disabling requires primary
confirmation plus an authenticator or recovery code. Password reset does not
disable 2FA. Enable and disable invalidate older sessions and delegated grants
using existing membership session versions.

### Existing account migration

Apply `0008_native_accounts.sql` and `0009_remove_auth_usernames.sql` before deploying this code. They reject ambiguous legacy emails that differ only in case (reconcile those identities before retrying migration), preserve tenant IDs, memberships, triggers and encrypted Linear connections, and backfill explicit Linear organization-to-workspace mappings. Existing Linear-only users choose **Forgot password or previously signed in with Linear?**, receive a reset email at their existing address, and set a password. Email possession is required; signup cannot replace an existing account's credentials. Existing native users keep their passwords and may sign in by email; unverified accounts must verify first. A reset never promotes a member to owner. An account with multiple existing owner memberships currently opens the oldest workspace; no new workspace-switching UI is introduced.

Linear OAuth requires an authenticated owner, binds state to that user/workspace, stores the connection there, and never creates a Factorize session. A Linear organization already bound to another workspace cannot be claimed. Existing webhook routes resolve the explicit mapping. Do not delete that binding to work around an account-recovery problem.

### Authentication verification

`npm run check` runs unit/contract tests and Postmark preflight tests. CI also runs the real PostgreSQL authentication suite against a disposable service. To run it locally, set `AUTH_TEST_DATABASE_URL` to an isolated PostgreSQL server whose user can create/drop test databases, then run `npm test --workspace=factorize -- --run test/native-auth.postgres.test.ts`. The suite creates and removes its own database and applies every migration, including a legacy connection fixture before the auth migration.

## Configure Cloudflare REST OAuth

Register a Cloudflare OAuth client using the authorization code and refresh
token grants, `client_secret_post`, and the exact callback
`<APP_ORIGIN>/oauth/cloudflare/callback`. Verify the application domain and
promote the client to public if users outside your account need to connect.

Set `CLOUDFLARE_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID`, `CLOUDFLARE_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET`, and
`CLOUDFLARE_OAUTH_DEFAULT_SCOPES` on the Worker. Defaults are a space-separated
list of scope IDs registered on the Cloudflare client. If the new scope setting
is absent, Factorize uses the existing `CLOUDFLARE_OAUTH_READ_SCOPES` setting.
Factorize normalizes whitespace, removes duplicates, and sends those defaults
and the `offline_access` protocol scope. Cloudflare validates the requested IDs.
Changing or removing defaults only affects new connection attempts, not saved
grants. Code exchange and refresh still require the OAuth client credentials.
Cloudflare chooses the eligible accounts and lets users review requested
permissions and decline or re-enable optional ones. To offer additional
permissions, update both the Cloudflare client and the configured defaults;
the consent screen does not add unrequested scopes.

After authorizing on Cloudflare, use `request_api` with paths relative to the
Cloudflare v4 REST API (for example, `/zones`). Cloudflare enforces the scopes
and accounts in the token. Factorize applies its usual connection access
controls and keeps the credentials server-side. Earlier account-bound
connections require a fresh authorization before using this proxy; stored
connection rows are retained, and existing agent grants do not transfer.
**Delete** removes Factorize's saved credentials; revoke the authorization on
Cloudflare to remove it there too.

Cloudflare Tail is retired. Old webhook endpoints return HTTP 410 and
Factorize no longer delivers Tail events. Historical configuration and Event
occurrences remain available for inspection or removal. The REST API integration
does not add log streaming or log triggers.

## Configure Linear

Use authorization-code OAuth and enable **Webhooks** on the OAuth application. Configure:

| Setting | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Callback URL | `https://your-domain.example/auth/linear/callback` |
| Webhook URL | `https://your-domain.example/webhooks/linear` |
| Webhook events | **Issues** and **Issue labels** |
| Webhook secret | Store as `LINEAR_WEBHOOK_SIGNING_SECRET` |

After changing the webhook settings, re-authorize existing workspaces so Linear creates a fresh workspace subscription.

## Configure ClickUp

Create a ClickUp OAuth application with the callback URL `https://your-domain.example/auth/clickup/callback`, then store its client ID and secret in `CLICKUP_CLIENT_ID` and `CLICKUP_CLIENT_SECRET`. Connecting ClickUp from Integrations registers the signed task webhook automatically. ClickUp events can filter a list by status, tag, assignee, or creator; all configured rules must match.


## Configuration reference

| Variable | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `LINEAR_CLIENT_ID` | Linear OAuth client ID |
| `LINEAR_CLIENT_SECRET` | Linear OAuth client secret |
| `LINEAR_WEBHOOK_SIGNING_SECRET` | Verifies Linear webhook signatures |
| `CLICKUP_CLIENT_ID` | ClickUp OAuth client ID |
| `CLICKUP_CLIENT_SECRET` | ClickUp OAuth client secret; ClickUp also uses a per-installation webhook secret stored encrypted by Factorize |
| `CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY` | Base64-encoded 32-byte key for encrypted credentials |
| `SESSION_SIGNING_SECRET` | Independent secret for signed browser sessions |
| `APP_ORIGIN` | Public Worker origin, configured in `packages/api/wrangler.jsonc` |
| `OAUTH_KV` | KV binding containing OAuth clients, grants, refresh tokens, and revocation state |

Never commit `.dev.vars` or production secret values. The included `.dev.vars.example` is a safe template.

## Operations
Source: https://docs.factorize.sh/self-hosting/operations

Use the [deployment guide](https://docs.factorize.sh/self-hosting/deployment) and the repository's
package-migration runbook for release and rollback procedures. Keep API
migrations, generated OpenAPI, API client output, and static frontend aligned.

The API Worker processes schedules and inbound provider webhooks. Monitor Worker
errors, database connectivity, and provider delivery outcomes. Event occurrences
are durable database records; MCP notifications prompt clients to read them and
are not the persistence layer.

Before a release, run the repository's documented local validation against an
isolated database. Never point validation at production or a shared database.
